Lunar Site Navigator — evidence

For a chosen point on the Moon, the science core computes the local 360° terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation data and finds when the Sun and the Earth are above that horizon. This page shows those results with the method, reference frame, data version and validation status of every number.

Built from package(s) site-f5debe0fd2f3cdf7, site-29ad241e86f8307d, site-a4d3f54375701349. Numbers are read from the packages and are not recomputed on this page. The page needs no network connection.

de Gerlache crater rim crestMons Malapert (Malapert massif) summitShackleton crater rim crestMethodsDataCompare two sitesEvidence pageValidation
PROVISIONAL RESULTS, NOT FINAL: built from the result packages published in packages/ of the repository. Event times and visibility shares on real terrain are unverified against an independent source (see Validation). This page is rebuilt whenever the packages change.

What blocks the view at 2 m

Obstacles of the terrain horizon that hide the Sun or the Earth for time in which they would be visible over a smooth sphere through the site, largest cost first (timeline.blockers).

No obstacle costs visible time at this height.

All windows at 2 m

Each window is a set of time intervals in which its condition holds. "Clipped" means an interval touches the start or end of the computed range, so its true start or end is not known.

Methods behind the numbers

Each number above refers to one of these method cards. A status of unverified or synthetic means the number has not been checked against an independent source.

de Gerlache crater rim crest

horizon.elevation — Terrain horizon elevation analytic-test-passed
Definition
For each azimuth and observer height: the largest elevation angle, above the plane perpendicular to the radial direction at the site, of the straight line from the observer to any terrain point along the great circle of that azimuth, out to the search radius. Negative when the terrain horizon lies below the horizontal.
Algorithm
Great-circle rays on a sphere. Exact triangle observer - terrain point - centre of the Moon, tan(e) = (r_t cos g - r_o) / (r_t sin g), evaluated in a cancellation-free form; curvature is contained in the formula. Each ray is covered by a lattice of points half a pixel apart. Near the site every lattice point is evaluated on the finest data. Farther out the lattice is grouped into cells; a cell is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it can reach the horizon already found, otherwise it is walked point by point on the finest data. Crossings of the ray with the lines through pixel centres (the creases of the bilinear surface) are evaluated as well, and the leading points are refined by nested sampling. All observer heights share the same terrain evaluations.
Frame
local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere
Time scale
none
Data
lola:LDEM_80S_20M@V2.0+LDEM_60S_60M@V2.0
Parameters
{"azimuth_step_deg": 0.25, "cell_growth": 0.008726646259971648, "creases": "every crossing of an evaluated stretch of ray with a line through pixel centres is evaluated", "finest_pixel_m": 20.0, "first_point_m": 20.0, "inner_lattice_step_m": 2.5, "inner_zone_m": 200.0, "interpolation": "bilinear between pixel centres, finest product that covers the point", "lattice_step_m": 10.0, "max_cell_m": 2560.0, "max_range_m": 300000.0, "refinement": "4 rounds of 9 points around the leading points of each azimuth", "skipping": "a cell of a ray is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it reaches the horizon already found"}
Evidence
core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_smooth_sphere_horizon_depression: largest error 3.0e-12 deg (threshold 0.0005 deg), 6 sites incl. both poles and the longitude seam; core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_crater_rim_at_known_distance_and_height: largest error 2e-13 deg (threshold 0.001 deg); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_hill_appears_at_its_bearing_with_the_right_elevation: largest error 3.4e-8 deg against an independent 1-D solution (threshold 0.002 deg); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_nothing_is_missed_on_a_rough_gridded_surface: never below an exhaustive 1 m reference scan on a spiked synthetic raster (threshold 0.002 deg, 144 comparisons); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_nothing_is_missed_on_lola_data: never below an exhaustive 1 m reference scan on the LOLA 20 m and 60 m south-polar products (threshold 0.002 deg; 648 comparisons at 6 test points measured by script); Self-convergence on LOLA data: a four times finer search changes no value by more than 0.0006 deg (51 840 values); No comparison with an independent horizon product has been made yet.
Limits
The terrain is the bilinear surface through the DEM pixels: relief smaller than a pixel is absent, and a crest between pixels is cut. Within about 1 km of the site this, not the algorithm, limits the accuracy.
Azimuth sampling is 0.25 deg; an obstacle narrower than that between two rays is not seen.
Single high pixels of the DEM are taken at face value, whether they are terrain or noise.
Terrain beyond the search radius or beyond the data is not seen; error_bounds.far_field_max_deg states how much it could add.
The observer is a point at the given height above the DEM surface on the radial through the site; the lander body, local rocks and regolith relief are not modelled.
horizon.far_field_bound — Bound on unseen far terrain analytic-test-passed
Definition
far_field_max_deg: the largest amount, over all azimuths and observer heights, by which terrain beyond the reach of the rays could still raise the horizon, if no such terrain is higher than ceiling_height_m. 0 means the search radius is proven sufficient under that assumption. far_field_open_azimuth_fraction: share of azimuths with a non-zero bound. shortest_reach_m: shortest ray reach (search radius, or the edge of the data).
Algorithm
A point of height H at central angle g from an observer at radius r_o is seen at elevation atan2((R+H) cos g - r_o, (R+H) sin g), which grows with H and, beyond the tangent point, falls with g. The bound is that elevation for H = ceiling at the end of each ray, minus the horizon found, floored at zero.
Frame
local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere
Time scale
none

horizon.obstacles — Obstacles of the horizon profile analytic-test-passed
Definition
An obstacle is a run of neighbouring azimuths whose horizon is set by the same piece of terrain. obstacle_id gives, per observer height and azimuth, the index of the obstacle in the obstacles list (-1 where the horizon has no data). Each obstacle lists its azimuth range, the range of distances of its limiting points, and its peak: the azimuth at which its horizon elevation is largest, with the distance, coordinates and height of the limiting point there.
Algorithm
Two neighbouring azimuths belong to the same obstacle if the distances of their limiting points differ by no more than 10% of the smaller one or by no more than 50 m. The profile is treated as periodic. near_field marks a peak closer than 1000 m.
Frame
local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere
Time scale
none
Data
lola:LDEM_80S_20M@V2.0+LDEM_60S_60M@V2.0
Parameters

terrain.patch — Terrain patch for drawing analytic-test-passed
Definition
up_m: the up coordinate, in the site's local East/North/Up frame and measured from the ground point of the site, of the surface point whose east and north coordinates are those of the grid node. The curvature of the sphere is in the values: on a smooth sphere they fall off as -(east^2 + north^2) / (2 r). NaN where the elevation data ends.
Algorithm
For every node the surface point is found whose position in the site frame has the node's east and north coordinates: its distance from the centre is the reference radius plus the terrain height at its latitude and longitude, settled by iteration to 0.1 mm. The terrain is read by bilinear interpolation from the block-average level of the elevation product whose pixel is the coarsest not larger than the grid spacing (sources lists product, level and checksum).

Limits
For drawing only. The horizon, the windows and the event times of the package are computed on the finest elevation data; a viewer must not derive visibility from this surface.
A coarse patch shows ground averaged over its grid cells: ridge crests are lower and narrow gaps are filled. Measured at three site records, the horizon of the drawn surface differs from the package horizon by up to 0.46 deg (terrain within 500 m of the site) and by up to 0.22 deg for terrain beyond 500 m; where they differ, the package horizon is right.
The grid is regular in the tangent plane of the site, not on the sphere: 32 km away a cell covers 0.02 % more ground than at the site. Overhangs cannot be represented.
Terrain beyond the largest patch is not in the package as a surface; its silhouette is in the horizon profile with the distance of the limiting terrain.

timeline.events — Rise and set events analytic-test-passed
Definition
Instants at which the visibility condition of the body (the 'threshold' of the event) starts or stops holding. 'visible_fraction > 0' means the first or last part of the disc (upper limb); 'margin_deg > 0' means the centre of the disc.
Algorithm
The governing signal (upper-limb margin, centre margin, lower-limb margin or visible fraction) is sampled every 60 s; every change of sign is located by bisection until the bracket is at most 0.5 s wide; the middle of the bracket is reported. The closing rate is the change of the governing margin over +/-30 s. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.

timeline.horizon_error — Band for a stated horizon error analytic-test-passed
Definition
visible_certain: the times at which the body is visible even if the terrain horizon is higher than computed by the stated angle. visible_possible: the times at which it is visible if the horizon is lower by that angle. visible_uncertain: possible and not certain. For every rise and set, earliest and latest give the interval of the uncertain set that contains the event.
Algorithm
The event finder is run on the horizon profile raised and lowered by the stated error: a common angle at every azimuth (horizon_error_deg), and/or atan(dem_height_error_m / distance of the limiting terrain) per azimuth, which is wide for near terrain and narrow for far terrain. Raising a horizon can only hide and lowering it can only reveal, so certain lies inside the nominal window and the nominal window inside possible.

Limits
The same sign is assumed at every azimuth. Real errors differ from azimuth to azimuth; the band is the unfavourable case for one event and says little about how errors along the profile combine.

Where the body grazes the horizon, a small angle moves an event by many hours; events can appear or disappear inside the band, and then the nominal event keeps its own time as both bounds.

timeline.lit_fraction — Lit fraction of the Sun's disc analytic-test-passed
Definition
Fraction of the area of the Sun's disc that is above the terrain horizon and not hidden by the Earth, 0 to 1. Outside an eclipse of the Sun by the Earth it equals the visible fraction. Stored for the Sun only.
Algorithm
At the samples inside an eclipse (between the first and the last contact at the site) the part of the disc hidden by the Earth is subtracted from the visible fraction: in each of the 63 strips, the overlap of the Earth's disc with what the horizon left visible, integrated on 511 finer strips because the Earth's limb is steep where it crosses the Sun. The Earth is an opaque disc of its equatorial radius, without atmosphere. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.

timeline.opportunity — Landing windows of a stated requirement and slip tolerance analytic-test-passed
Definition
landing_windows: the set of landing times for which every condition of the requirement holds. slip_tolerance_s: how long the planned landing can be delayed while the requirement keeps holding (0 if the planned time is not feasible); early_tolerance_s: how much earlier it can be. wait_s: time from an infeasible planned landing to the next landing window. feasible_s_per_period: feasible landing time inside each lunar day.

Exact interval arithmetic on the visibility windows: erosion of the windows for 'continuous from landing', a piecewise-linear cumulative measure for 'total in mission', intersection of all conditions. No sampling of dates.

timeline.station_links — Direct-to-Earth windows per ground station and relay need analytic-test-passed
Definition
A two-way link with a station is geometrically possible when the station (a point on the Earth) is above the terrain horizon of the site and the site is at least 10 deg above the station's horizon; 'receive' uses 6 deg. The network window is the union over the three Deep Space Network complexes, each represented by its 70 m antenna. Relay need: 0 direct link possible at all times; 1 interrupted only by station gaps; 2 interrupted by lunar terrain for part of the time; 3 no station ever above the lunar terrain.
Algorithm
Station positions and local verticals relative to the Moon's centre, tabulated every 600 s in the Moon body-fixed frame (SPICE, LT+S) and interpolated; both conditions sampled every 120 s; changes located by bisection to 0.5 s. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.

timeline.visible_fraction — Visible fraction of the disc analytic-test-passed
Definition
Fraction of the area of the disc that is above the horizon, 0 to 1. The disc is uniform (no limb darkening).
Algorithm
The disc is cut into 63 vertical strips (Gauss-Chebyshev nodes of the second kind); in each strip the part above the horizon at the strip's azimuth is taken exactly; the strips are summed with their area weights. timeline.windows — Visibility windows analytic-test-passed
Definition
Intervals during which the stated condition holds. '*_visible' uses the scenario threshold; '*_any_part_visible' and '*_full_disc_visible' bracket the partial phase: between them the disc is partly hidden and 'visible_fraction' says how much. 'sun_eclipsed_by_earth' and 'sun_totally_eclipsed_by_earth' are eclipses of the Sun by the Earth seen from the site; 'sun_lit' is 'sun_any_part_visible' without the total eclipses.
Algorithm
Built from the refined event times; 'sun_and_earth_visible' is the intersection of the two '*_visible' sets. Eclipse contacts: the separation of the Sun and the Earth seen from the site equals the sum (partial) or the difference (total) of their angular radii; Earth as an opaque disc of its equatorial radius without atmosphere; located by bisection like the events. A window that touches the start or the end of the computed range is marked clipped.

horizon.elevation — Terrain horizon elevation analytic-test-passed
Definition
For each azimuth and observer height: the largest elevation angle, above the plane perpendicular to the radial direction at the site, of the straight line from the observer to any terrain point along the great circle of that azimuth, out to the search radius. Negative when the terrain horizon lies below the horizontal.
Algorithm
Great-circle rays on a sphere. Exact triangle observer - terrain point - centre of the Moon, tan(e) = (r_t cos g - r_o) / (r_t sin g), evaluated in a cancellation-free form; curvature is contained in the formula. Each ray is covered by a lattice of points half a pixel apart. Near the site every lattice point is evaluated on the finest data. Farther out the lattice is grouped into cells; a cell is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it can reach the horizon already found, otherwise it is walked point by point on the finest data. Crossings of the ray with the lines through pixel centres (the creases of the bilinear surface) are evaluated as well, and the leading points are refined by nested sampling. All observer heights share the same terrain evaluations.
Frame
local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere
Time scale
none
Data

Parameters

Limits
The terrain is the bilinear surface through the DEM pixels: relief smaller than a pixel is absent, and a crest between pixels is cut. Within about 1 km of the site this, not the algorithm, limits the accuracy.
Azimuth sampling is 0.25 deg; an obstacle narrower than that between two rays is not seen.
Single high pixels of the DEM are taken at face value, whether they are terrain or noise.
Terrain beyond the search radius or beyond the data is not seen; error_bounds.far_field_max_deg states how much it could add.
The observer is a point at the given height above the DEM surface on the radial through the site; the lander body, local rocks and regolith relief are not modelled.
horizon.far_field_bound — Bound on unseen far terrain analytic-test-passed
Definition
far_field_max_deg: the largest amount, over all azimuths and observer heights, by which terrain beyond the reach of the rays could still raise the horizon, if no such terrain is higher than ceiling_height_m. 0 means the search radius is proven sufficient under that assumption. far_field_open_azimuth_fraction: share of azimuths with a non-zero bound. shortest_reach_m: shortest ray reach (search radius, or the edge of the data).
Algorithm
A point of height H at central angle g from an observer at radius r_o is seen at elevation atan2((R+H) cos g - r_o, (R+H) sin g), which grows with H and, beyond the tangent point, falls with g. The bound is that elevation for H = ceiling at the end of each ray, minus the horizon found, floored at zero.

horizon.obstacles — Obstacles of the horizon profile analytic-test-passed
Definition
An obstacle is a run of neighbouring azimuths whose horizon is set by the same piece of terrain. obstacle_id gives, per observer height and azimuth, the index of the obstacle in the obstacles list (-1 where the horizon has no data). Each obstacle lists its azimuth range, the range of distances of its limiting points, and its peak: the azimuth at which its horizon elevation is largest, with the distance, coordinates and height of the limiting point there.
Algorithm
Two neighbouring azimuths belong to the same obstacle if the distances of their limiting points differ by no more than 10% of the smaller one or by no more than 50 m. The profile is treated as periodic. near_field marks a peak closer than 1000 m.

core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_smooth_sphere_horizon_depression: largest error 3.0e-12 deg (threshold 0.0005 deg), 6 sites incl. both poles and the longitude seam; core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_crater_rim_at_known_distance_and_height: largest error 2e-13 deg (threshold 0.001 deg); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_hill_appears_at_its_bearing_with_the_right_elevation: largest error 3.4e-8 deg against an independent 1-D solution (threshold 0.002 deg); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_nothing_is_missed_on_a_rough_gridded_surface: never below an exhaustive 1 m reference scan on a spiked synthetic raster (threshold 0.002 deg, 144 comparisons); core/tests/test_horizon.py::test_nothing_is_missed_on_lola_data: never below an exhaustive 1 m reference scan on the LOLA 20 m and 60 m south-polar products (threshold 0.002 deg; 648 comparisons at 6 test points measured by script); Self-convergence on LOLA data: a four times finer search changes no value by more than 0.0006 deg (51 840 values); No comparison with an independent horizon product has been made yet.
Limits
The terrain is the bilinear surface through the DEM pixels: relief smaller than a pixel is absent, and a crest between pixels is cut. Within about 1 km of the site this, not the algorithm, limits the accuracy.
Azimuth sampling is 0.25 deg; an obstacle narrower than that between two rays is not seen.
Single high pixels of the DEM are taken at face value, whether they are terrain or noise.
Terrain beyond the search radius or beyond the data is not seen; error_bounds.far_field_max_deg states how much it could add.
The observer is a point at the given height above the DEM surface on the radial through the site; the lander body, local rocks and regolith relief are not modelled.
terrain.patch — Terrain patch for drawing analytic-test-passed
Definition
up_m: the up coordinate, in the site's local East/North/Up frame and measured from the ground point of the site, of the surface point whose east and north coordinates are those of the grid node. The curvature of the sphere is in the values: on a smooth sphere they fall off as -(east^2 + north^2) / (2 r). NaN where the elevation data ends.
Algorithm
For every node the surface point is found whose position in the site frame has the node's east and north coordinates: its distance from the centre is the reference radius plus the terrain height at its latitude and longitude, settled by iteration to 0.1 mm. The terrain is read by bilinear interpolation from the block-average level of the elevation product whose pixel is the coarsest not larger than the grid spacing (sources lists product, level and checksum).

local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere; origin at the ground point of the site

Limits
For drawing only. The horizon, the windows and the event times of the package are computed on the finest elevation data; a viewer must not derive visibility from this surface.
A coarse patch shows ground averaged over its grid cells: ridge crests are lower and narrow gaps are filled. Measured at three site records, the horizon of the drawn surface differs from the package horizon by up to 0.46 deg (terrain within 500 m of the site) and by up to 0.22 deg for terrain beyond 500 m; where they differ, the package horizon is right.
The grid is regular in the tangent plane of the site, not on the sphere: 32 km away a cell covers 0.02 % more ground than at the site. Overhangs cannot be represented.
Terrain beyond the largest patch is not in the package as a surface; its silhouette is in the horizon profile with the distance of the limiting terrain.

timeline.events — Rise and set events analytic-test-passed
Definition
Instants at which the visibility condition of the body (the 'threshold' of the event) starts or stops holding. 'visible_fraction > 0' means the first or last part of the disc (upper limb); 'margin_deg > 0' means the centre of the disc.
Algorithm
The governing signal (upper-limb margin, centre margin, lower-limb margin or visible fraction) is sampled every 60 s; every change of sign is located by bisection until the bracket is at most 0.5 s wide; the middle of the bracket is reported. timeline.horizon_error — Band for a stated horizon error analytic-test-passed
Definition
visible_certain: the times at which the body is visible even if the terrain horizon is higher than computed by the stated angle. visible_possible: the times at which it is visible if the horizon is lower by that angle. visible_uncertain: possible and not certain. For every rise and set, earliest and latest give the interval of the uncertain set that contains the event.
Algorithm
The event finder is run on the horizon profile raised and lowered by the stated error: a common angle at every azimuth (horizon_error_deg), and/or atan(dem_height_error_m / distance of the limiting terrain) per azimuth, which is wide for near terrain and narrow for far terrain. Raising a horizon can only hide and lowering it can only reveal, so certain lies inside the nominal window and the nominal window inside possible.

The same sign is assumed at every azimuth. Real errors differ from azimuth to azimuth; the band is the unfavourable case for one event and says little about how errors along the profile combine.

timeline.lit_fraction — Lit fraction of the Sun's disc analytic-test-passed
Definition
Fraction of the area of the Sun's disc that is above the terrain horizon and not hidden by the Earth, 0 to 1. Outside an eclipse of the Sun by the Earth it equals the visible fraction. Stored for the Sun only.
Algorithm
At the samples inside an eclipse (between the first and the last contact at the site) the part of the disc hidden by the Earth is subtracted from the visible fraction: in each of the 63 strips, the overlap of the Earth's disc with what the horizon left visible, integrated on 511 finer strips because the Earth's limb is steep where it crosses the Sun. timeline.station_links — Direct-to-Earth windows per ground station and relay need analytic-test-passed
Definition
A two-way link with a station is geometrically possible when the station (a point on the Earth) is above the terrain horizon of the site and the site is at least 10 deg above the station's horizon; 'receive' uses 6 deg. The network window is the union over the three Deep Space Network complexes, each represented by its 70 m antenna. Relay need: 0 direct link possible at all times; 1 interrupted only by station gaps; 2 interrupted by lunar terrain for part of the time; 3 no station ever above the lunar terrain.
Algorithm
Station positions and local verticals relative to the Moon's centre, tabulated every 600 s in the Moon body-fixed frame (SPICE, LT+S) and interpolated; both conditions sampled every 120 s; changes located by bisection to 0.5 s. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.

timeline.visible_fraction — Visible fraction of the disc analytic-test-passed
Definition
Fraction of the area of the disc that is above the horizon, 0 to 1. The disc is uniform (no limb darkening).
Algorithm
The disc is cut into 63 vertical strips (Gauss-Chebyshev nodes of the second kind); in each strip the part above the horizon at the strip's azimuth is taken exactly; the strips are summed with their area weights. The horizon is the terrain horizon profile of this package, linearly interpolated in azimuth.

timeline.windows — Visibility windows analytic-test-passed
Definition
Intervals during which the stated condition holds. '*_visible' uses the scenario threshold; '*_any_part_visible' and '*_full_disc_visible' bracket the partial phase: between them the disc is partly hidden and 'visible_fraction' says how much. 'sun_eclipsed_by_earth' and 'sun_totally_eclipsed_by_earth' are eclipses of the Sun by the Earth seen from the site; 'sun_lit' is 'sun_any_part_visible' without the total eclipses.
Algorithm
Built from the refined event times; 'sun_and_earth_visible' is the intersection of the two '*_visible' sets. Eclipse contacts: the separation of the Sun and the Earth seen from the site equals the sum (partial) or the difference (total) of their angular radii; Earth as an opaque disc of its equatorial radius without atmosphere; located by bisection like the events. A window that touches the start or the end of the computed range is marked clipped.

horizon.elevation — Terrain horizon elevation analytic-test-passed
Definition
For each azimuth and observer height: the largest elevation angle, above the plane perpendicular to the radial direction at the site, of the straight line from the observer to any terrain point along the great circle of that azimuth, out to the search radius. Negative when the terrain horizon lies below the horizontal.
Algorithm
Great-circle rays on a sphere. Exact triangle observer - terrain point - centre of the Moon, tan(e) = (r_t cos g - r_o) / (r_t sin g), evaluated in a cancellation-free form; curvature is contained in the formula. Each ray is covered by a lattice of points half a pixel apart. Near the site every lattice point is evaluated on the finest data. Farther out the lattice is grouped into cells; a cell is skipped only if the block maximum of the terrain over the cell proves that nothing in it can reach the horizon already found, otherwise it is walked point by point on the finest data. Crossings of the ray with the lines through pixel centres (the creases of the bilinear surface) are evaluated as well, and the leading points are refined by nested sampling. All observer heights share the same terrain evaluations.
Frame
local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere
Time scale

horizon.far_field_bound — Bound on unseen far terrain analytic-test-passed
Definition
far_field_max_deg: the largest amount, over all azimuths and observer heights, by which terrain beyond the reach of the rays could still raise the horizon, if no such terrain is higher than ceiling_height_m. 0 means the search radius is proven sufficient under that assumption. far_field_open_azimuth_fraction: share of azimuths with a non-zero bound. shortest_reach_m: shortest ray reach (search radius, or the edge of the data).
Algorithm
A point of height H at central angle g from an observer at radius r_o is seen at elevation atan2((R+H) cos g - r_o, (R+H) sin g), which grows with H and, beyond the tangent point, falls with g. The bound is that elevation for H = ceiling at the end of each ray, minus the horizon found, floored at zero.

horizon.obstacles — Obstacles of the horizon profile analytic-test-passed
Definition
An obstacle is a run of neighbouring azimuths whose horizon is set by the same piece of terrain. obstacle_id gives, per observer height and azimuth, the index of the obstacle in the obstacles list (-1 where the horizon has no data). Each obstacle lists its azimuth range, the range of distances of its limiting points, and its peak: the azimuth at which its horizon elevation is largest, with the distance, coordinates and height of the limiting point there.
Algorithm
Two neighbouring azimuths belong to the same obstacle if the distances of their limiting points differ by no more than 10% of the smaller one or by no more than 50 m. The profile is treated as periodic. near_field marks a peak closer than 1000 m.

terrain.patch — Terrain patch for drawing analytic-test-passed
Definition
up_m: the up coordinate, in the site's local East/North/Up frame and measured from the ground point of the site, of the surface point whose east and north coordinates are those of the grid node. The curvature of the sphere is in the values: on a smooth sphere they fall off as -(east^2 + north^2) / (2 r). NaN where the elevation data ends.
Algorithm
For every node the surface point is found whose position in the site frame has the node's east and north coordinates: its distance from the centre is the reference radius plus the terrain height at its latitude and longitude, settled by iteration to 0.1 mm. The terrain is read by bilinear interpolation from the block-average level of the elevation product whose pixel is the coarsest not larger than the grid spacing (sources lists product, level and checksum).

local East/North/Up at the site; up is the outward radial direction of the reference sphere; origin at the ground point of the site

Limits
For drawing only. The horizon, the windows and the event times of the package are computed on the finest elevation data; a viewer must not derive visibility from this surface.
A coarse patch shows ground averaged over its grid cells: ridge crests are lower and narrow gaps are filled. Measured at three site records, the horizon of the drawn surface differs from the package horizon by up to 0.46 deg (terrain within 500 m of the site) and by up to 0.22 deg for terrain beyond 500 m; where they differ, the package horizon is right.
The grid is regular in the tangent plane of the site, not on the sphere: 32 km away a cell covers 0.02 % more ground than at the site. Overhangs cannot be represented.
Terrain beyond the largest patch is not in the package as a surface; its silhouette is in the horizon profile with the distance of the limiting terrain.
timeline.blocking — Time lost to terrain and the obstacle that causes it analytic-test-passed
Definition
lost_to_terrain: the times at which the body is visible over a smooth sphere and not visible over the terrain. gained_from_terrain: visible over the terrain and not over a smooth sphere (terrain below the smooth horizon). blocker_azimuth_index: for every sample of the series, the index of the horizon sample that limits the view of the disc; for a hidden disc under the 'any part visible' condition it is where the disc is closest to showing. blockers: the lost time split between the obstacles of the horizon, each with the intervals in which it is the limiting obstacle.

Interval algebra on the visibility windows (lost = smooth AND NOT terrain). For the split, each sample of the series stands for the half step before and after it, and its time goes to the obstacle at its limiting horizon sample.

timeline.events — Rise and set events analytic-test-passed
Definition
Instants at which the visibility condition of the body (the 'threshold' of the event) starts or stops holding. 'visible_fraction > 0' means the first or last part of the disc (upper limb); 'margin_deg > 0' means the centre of the disc.

The governing signal (upper-limb margin, centre margin, lower-limb margin or visible fraction) is sampled every 60 s; every change of sign is located by bisection until the bracket is at most 0.5 s wide; the middle of the bracket is reported. timeline.horizon_error — Band for a stated horizon error analytic-test-passed
Definition
visible_certain: the times at which the body is visible even if the terrain horizon is higher than computed by the stated angle. visible_possible: the times at which it is visible if the horizon is lower by that angle. visible_uncertain: possible and not certain. For every rise and set, earliest and latest give the interval of the uncertain set that contains the event.
Algorithm
The event finder is run on the horizon profile raised and lowered by the stated error: a common angle at every azimuth (horizon_error_deg), and/or atan(dem_height_error_m / distance of the limiting terrain) per azimuth, which is wide for near terrain and narrow for far terrain. Raising a horizon can only hide and lowering it can only reveal, so certain lies inside the nominal window and the nominal window inside possible.

The same sign is assumed at every azimuth. Real errors differ from azimuth to azimuth; the band is the unfavourable case for one event and says little about how errors along the profile combine.

The stated numbers are inputs, not estimates of the elevation model's accuracy.
Ephemeris, landing position and observer height are not in this band.
Where the body grazes the horizon, a small angle moves an event by many hours; events can appear or disappear inside the band, and then the nominal event keeps its own time as both bounds.

timeline.lit_fraction — Lit fraction of the Sun's disc analytic-test-passed
Definition
Fraction of the area of the Sun's disc that is above the terrain horizon and not hidden by the Earth, 0 to 1. Outside an eclipse of the Sun by the Earth it equals the visible fraction. Stored for the Sun only.
Algorithm
At the samples inside an eclipse (between the first and the last contact at the site) the part of the disc hidden by the Earth is subtracted from the visible fraction: in each of the 63 strips, the overlap of the Earth's disc with what the horizon left visible, integrated on 511 finer strips because the Earth's limb is steep where it crosses the Sun. timeline.station_links — Direct-to-Earth windows per ground station and relay need analytic-test-passed
Definition
A two-way link with a station is geometrically possible when the station (a point on the Earth) is above the terrain horizon of the site and the site is at least 10 deg above the station's horizon; 'receive' uses 6 deg. The network window is the union over the three Deep Space Network complexes, each represented by its 70 m antenna. Relay need: 0 direct link possible at all times; 1 interrupted only by station gaps; 2 interrupted by lunar terrain for part of the time; 3 no station ever above the lunar terrain.
Algorithm
Station positions and local verticals relative to the Moon's centre, tabulated every 600 s in the Moon body-fixed frame (SPICE, LT+S) and interpolated; both conditions sampled every 120 s; changes located by bisection to 0.5 s. timeline.windows — Visibility windows analytic-test-passed
Definition
Intervals during which the stated condition holds. '*_visible' uses the scenario threshold; '*_any_part_visible' and '*_full_disc_visible' bracket the partial phase: between them the disc is partly hidden and 'visible_fraction' says how much. Built from the refined event times; 'sun_and_earth_visible' is the intersection of the two '*_visible' sets. Not validated

  • Individual rise and set times on real terrain not validated
    The long-term shares of lit and Earth-visible time agree with the published LOLA maps on terrain of the same resolution; of the two checks against dated images one agrees and one fails its criterion; and no independent source gives the time of a sunrise or sunset at a point on real terrain. Where an event is set by terrain closer than about 1 km, the elevation grid limits its accuracy.
  • The elevation model itself not validated here
    Every terrain check on this card uses LOLA elevation data on both sides. The data stream checks the georeferencing of the LOLA files separately.
  • Exact rise and set times at a real lander not available
    No source examined for Blue Ghost Mission 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1 or IM-2 prints a sunrise or sunset clock time for the landing site. Operational records (hours of daylight, expected wake-up date) only bound the computed events from one side.
  • Direct-to-Earth windows geometry validated, windows not
    Both ends of the link geometry agree with Horizons. The windows built from them, the station elevation limits as single numbers (no azimuth-dependent masks), and anything about link budget, multipath or scheduling have not been compared with an external source.
  • Earth rise and set against an independent source not done
    Horizons does not state which point of the Earth's disc its rise and set refer to; only the Earth's direction and size are validated.
  • Sunlight during an eclipse partly modelled
    Eclipses of the Sun by the Earth are computed for an opaque Earth without atmosphere and checked against one published eclipse. The light that the Earth's atmosphere refracts into the shadow, and any measured power curve of a lander, are not modelled or compared.

Limits

  • Near the lunar poles the terrain horizon, not the ephemeris, sets the accuracy of an event time: a horizon error of 0.01 deg can move an event by many minutes. The terrain checks on this card test long-term shares and two dated images, not event times.
  • The external reference (Horizons) and the core use JPL ephemerides of the same family; an error common to both would not show.
  • Thresholds marked as written in the acceptance test were committed in the same commit as the code they test; the thresholds of the comparisons with external sources have commits of their own that predate the data or the computation, as listed above.
  • The lander and eclipse comparisons are not blind: earlier research had compared some of the published values with Horizons.

Team Kestro Aerospace, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Source code and data provenance: https://github.com/Littiary/lunar-site-navigator. Candidate sites are the project's own points, not official landing sites.
